title: Keeping alpacas on a smallholding
subtitle: What alpacas need and how they fit into a mixed smallholding system.
excerpt: Alpacas are smallholding livestock for fibre, companionship, and sometimes guard duty alongside sheep. They need less housing than most livestock, are easy fencers to contain, and require shearing once a year. The main considerations before buying are space, companion numbers (they must be kept in groups of at least three), and the annual husbandry calendar.
sourceNotes: British Alpaca Society, Guide to Keeping Alpacas (2022). DEFRA, Alpaca and Llama Code of Practice (2009). David and Kay Spalding, Alpacas for the Small Farm (2017).

glossaryTerms.definition: A newborn or young alpaca, from birth to approximately 6 months of age.
The unit used to measure fibre diameter in alpaca fleece. Finer fibre (lower micron) is softer and more valuable. Huacaya cria fibre is typically 15 to 20 microns.

content.text: Alpacas are herd animals from the Andean altiplano. They are quiet, intelligent, and relatively hardy in the UK climate. A minimum of three animals is the welfare standard; a lone alpaca or a pair may suffer from social stress. Buying a group of three to five established animals is the most straightforward start.

The British Alpaca Society recommends approximately 1 acre (0.4 hectare) for 5 to 6 alpacas on good pasture, with rotation. Alpacas graze with very low impact compared to sheep or horses, and rarely damage pasture. Fencing needs to be 1.2 m high to contain them reliably; standard stock netting (C8 grade or similar) at that height works well. Barbed wire is not suitable.

Alpacas tolerate cold and wet if they have access to a dry, draught-free shelter. A three-sided field shelter open to the south, with at least 4 m2 per animal, is adequate for UK conditions. They do not need heated housing but must have cover during persistent heavy rain: their thick fibre becomes saturated and they take a long time to dry. Alpacas with no access to shelter in wet conditions can develop hypothermia.
Good-quality pasture is the main feed source from spring to autumn. Supplement with meadow hay in winter or when grazing is poor.
An alpaca mineral supplement is important; UK forage is often short of selenium and copper. Use a camelid product, not sheep minerals.
Ensure fresh water is always available. Alpacas drink less than sheep of similar body weight but still need a minimum 5 litres per day.
Spring (April/May): shearing and toe-nail trimming. Record
results if you want to track fibre quality over years.
the following spring. Check for BCS; alpacas are easy to over-condition on lush summer pasture.
Autumn: worm, vaccinate against clostridial disease and pasteurella, and check body condition. Top up hay as pasture declines.
Winter: monitor body condition closely. Pregnant females in the last third of pregnancy need supplementary feed.

attrs.cue: Alpacas are humming constantly and appear stressed
attrs.cause: Social disruption, separation from herd mates, or the presence of a perceived threat (dog, unfamiliar animal)
attrs.fix: Humming is normal alpaca communication; constant distressed humming is different. Check that the whole group is together. Remove the stressor if identifiable.

attrs.cue: Animal appears thin despite good grazing
attrs.cause: High worm burden, selenium deficiency, or dental problems preventing adequate feed intake
attrs.fix: Perform faecal egg count. Have the teeth checked by a camelid-experienced vet. Test blood selenium levels; camelid selenium deficiency is common in the UK on unfortified pasture.
